summary: Proposes interfaces for a Signaling Gateway that connects switched circuit networks, such as telephone networks, to IP networks, as defined by Tekelec's Transport Adapter Layer Interface. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This describes how a translator box lets old phone networks and the Internet pass signals to each other.

questions: how to carry ss7 over ip networks
subtitle: Bridging telephone networks and IP networks with SS7 signaling over TCP/IP

tldr.problem: Traditional telephone networks use SS7 signaling over dedicated links, while IP networks have different transport mechanisms. Connecting these two network types requires a translation layer.
tldr.mechanism: TALI encapsulates SS7 signaling messages (such as TCAP, ISUP, and MTP) inside TCP/IP packets, allowing signaling gateways to bridge switched circuit networks and IP networks without changing the original protocols.
tldr.outcome: TALI enables converged networks where devices from both traditional PSTN and IP networks can communicate through signaling gateways, supporting the gradual transition to IP-based telecommunications.

today: RFC 3094 is an Informational RFC documenting Tekelec's vendor-specific proposal for carrying SS7 over IP. It was published in April 2001 as a response to standards-track work in the IETF SIGTRAN working group. As an alternative design rather than a standard, TALI saw adoption in some vendor products but the IETF standardized different protocols like SCTP and SigTran (which are now standards track).

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 3094 defines the Transport Adapter Layer Interface (TALI), a protocol created by Tekelec to carry SS7 signaling over IP networks. SS7 (Signaling System 7) is the protocol used by the traditional public switched telephone network (PSTN) to control calls and manage network functions.

As networks converge and IP becomes the dominant transport, TALI provides a bridge between legacy PSTN equipment and modern IP-based systems. The protocol sits between the SS7 layers and the TCP/IP stack, encapsulating signaling messages so they can travel across IP networks.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC describes how to send old-style telephone control signals through modern Internet networks so that telephone companies and internet devices can understand each other.

sections.title: Traditional and Converged Network Architecture
sections.content:
Traditional PSTN networks consist of three types of devices connected by dedicated signaling links: SSPs (Signaling Service Points, the endpoints), STPs (Signaling Transfer Points, the switches), and SCPs (Signaling Control Points, the databases). Each link carries SS7 traffic over dedicated lines using MTP-2 and MTP-1 protocols.

In a converged network, new IP-based devices emerge: Signaling Gateways (SGs) that translate between PSTN and IP networks, Media Gateway Controllers (MGCs) that manage the conversion of voice traffic, and Media Gateways (MGs) that handle the actual voice streams. TALI enables communication between SGs and MGCs, between SGs themselves, and between SGs and IP-based service control points.
sections.plainLanguage: Old phone networks have special switches and computers that talk to each other over private phone lines. New networks put similar devices on the Internet instead, and TALI helps the old and new devices speak to each other.

sections.title: TALI Message Structure
sections.content:
Every TALI message starts with a 10-byte header followed by optional data. The header consists of:

  • SYNC (4 bytes): always the ASCII text "TALI"
  • OPCODE (4 bytes): a 4-byte ASCII code identifying the message type
  • LENGTH (2 bytes): the size of the data payload

Version 1.0 defines several opcode types: test and moni for peer-to-peer messages, allo and proh for controlling whether a connection carries SS7 traffic, and service messages like sccp, isot (ISUP over TALI), and mtp3 to carry different SS7 protocol layers. Version 2.0 adds new opcodes for management operations and extended services.
sections.plainLanguage: Each message is like an envelope with a label showing what is inside and how big it is.

sections.title: Connection States and Control
sections.content:
A TALI connection is established over a single TCP socket between a client and server endpoint. Once the socket is open, both endpoints operate as peers, using the same send and receive calls.

TALI defines a state machine with peer-to-peer control messages. The allo message signals that one endpoint is ready to send service traffic; the proh message prohibits further traffic. The moni message acts as a keepalive and, in version 2.0, carries version identification so endpoints can detect whether the far end supports advanced features.

A set of timers (T1, T2, T3, T4) control timeouts for retransmission and monitoring. Management events allow external control: opening or closing the socket, allowing or prohibiting traffic, and gracefully shutting down the connection.
sections.plainLanguage: The connection works like a phone call: you dial to connect, you tell each other when you are ready to talk, and you hang up when done.

sections.title: Protocol Versions and Deployment
sections.content:
TALI defines two major versions. Version 1.0 is the baseline, carrying SS7 messaging with peer-to-peer control. It relies on TCP's own sequence numbering and cannot support SS7 changeover and changeback procedures, which require preserving sequence numbers from the MTP-2 layer.

Version 2.0 adds optional support for routing key registration, allowing dynamic circuit management, and for MTP3 primitives that provide additional network management capabilities. Version 2.0 maintains backward compatibility: a 2.0 implementation can communicate with a 1.0 node by detecting version support through the moni message format and limiting itself to 1.0 opcodes when talking to older implementations.

The RFC notes that TALI can be deployed over alternative transports like SAAL (for DS1 links) or SCTP (once that protocol matures), though TCP is the proven choice at the time of publication.
sections.plainLanguage: The protocol comes in two flavors: a simple version for basic message transport, and a fancy version with extra features for managing circuits and networks. Old and new versions can work together.
